identity.title: Scaling LLM Test-Time Compute Optimally Can be More Effective than Scaling Parameters for Reasoning

problem.claim: The paper asks how much a language model can improve on a challenging prompt when given a fixed, non-trivial amount of inference-time compute.

gap.claim: The authors state that test-time inference scaling behavior is little studied, with prior work largely reporting negative results for several strategies.

contributions.claim: Analyzes test-time scaling through searches against dense process-based verifier reward models and adaptive updates to the response distribution conditioned on the prompt.
Motivates a compute-optimal strategy that adaptively allocates test-time compute per prompt.
Reports that test-time compute can outperform parameter scaling under a FLOPs-matched evaluation in a specified smaller-model regime.

stated_novelty.claim: The authors distinguish their work by analyzing prompt-dependent effectiveness across two test-time computation mechanisms and using this variation to motivate compute-optimal allocation.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report that the effectiveness of test-time scaling approaches critically depends on prompt difficulty for both analyzed mechanisms.
The authors report over 4× greater efficiency than a best-of-N baseline for scaling test-time compute on math reasoning problems.
In a FLOPs-matched evaluation, the authors report that test-time compute outperforms a 14× larger model on problems where the smaller base model has somewhat non-trivial success rates.

narrative_sequence.summary: Frames improved outputs from additional test-time compute as relevant to self-improving agents.
Asks how much performance can improve under a fixed, non-trivial inference-compute budget, with implications for pretraining–inference tradeoffs.
Studies verifier-guided search and prompt-conditioned adaptive response-distribution updates.
Finds prompt-difficulty dependence and motivates adaptive compute-optimal allocation.
Reports over 4× efficiency versus best-of-N and superiority over a 14× larger model in a FLOPs-matched regime.

source_observation.claim: The abstract links variation by prompt difficulty to an adaptive strategy for allocating test-time compute.

lessons.interpretation: A method’s aggregate scaling result may conceal meaningful prompt-level heterogeneity; exposing that heterogeneity can motivate conditional resource allocation.
lessons.application: Report performance or compute allocation stratified by prompt difficulty, then test a difficulty-aware budget policy.
lessons.exception: This move may be unsuitable when prompt difficulty cannot be estimated reliably or when only a uniform-budget deployment is permitted.

unknowns: The abstract does not specify how prompt difficulty is measured or how compute-optimal allocation is implemented.
The reported 4× efficiency, 14× size comparison, FLOPs matching, and smaller-model success-rate regime lack detailed datasets, baselines, budgets, and statistical conditions.
The abstract does not establish whether the reported gains generalize beyond the stated math-reasoning and evaluation settings.
